Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 87, verses 1–5 (part 1 of 2):

The opening of the surah begins with a very gentle and long-drawn cadence; through this lengthened tone a pleasant and fragrant sound of tasbih (glorification) is spread through the atmosphere. After this comes the command to glorify, and then the attributes that have been brought after the glorification.

"Sabbih isma..." to "ahwa" (87:1–5): "(O Prophet!) Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and proportioned, who measured out and then guided, who brought forth the pasture and then made it dark, withered rubbish." The purpose is that through this tasbih the sound of glorification should echo in every corner and expanse of this whole universe, and the whole universe should appear as a place of worship (ma'bad), and, alongside being a place of worship, the whole universe should also become an exhibition hall of the products of the Creator's power.

"Alladhi... fahda" (87:3): "who created and proportioned, who measured out and then guided."

What are the meanings of tasbih? Keeping the supremacy of Allah in mind, regarding Allah as free from every defect, keeping the attributes of Allah's beautiful names (asma' al-husna) present in the mind, and keeping one's taste, intuition, heart and consciousness illuminated by the light, brightness and radiance of these things: this is what tasbih is called. Merely reciting "Subhan Allah" with the tongue is not called tasbih.

"Sabbih... al-a'la" (87:1): "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High." These words bring upon human intuition and consciousness a particular state. This intuitive state is of such a kind that its expression is not possible in words. It is indeed an intuitive and experiential matter, and it points to a kind of life that is connected with the remembrance of certain meanings and certain attributes, not with the rote memorization of words.

What are these meanings and attributes? The first attribute is the attribute of rububiyyah (lordship), and the second is that of al-a'la (the Most High). Rabb means nurturer, supervisor and sustainer. The shadows and reflections of these attributes are in harmony with the atmosphere of this surah and with the glad tidings expressed within it, especially with its gentle manner. The attribute al-a'la brings before the screen of consciousness images through which loftiness, supremacy, and a limitless and boundless horizon are expressed. The human soul glorifies (tasbih) far into the distance, and through this concept of loftiness, tasbih acquires a connection with purity and greatness, and tasbih, in terms of its basic elements, is the name of the concept of the loftiness of the Lord.

The initial address is clearly to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it is a direct address to him from Allah. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite this command of his Lord, "Sabbih" ("glorify"), he would act upon this command before reading the following verses, and would say: "Subhana Rabbiya al-a'la" ("I glorify my Lord, the Most High"). Thus the command and the response to the command, or the fulfilment of the command, would take place, the obedience to the command would be accomplished, and there would be a supplication and a question-and-answer with Allah. Because the Messenger stood before his Lord, he was receiving this speech directly from the Lord, and in that state of connection and closeness he would give the response. When these verses were revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) instructed the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) to recite this tasbih in prostration. (Ij'alūhā fī sujūdikum – "Make it in your prostrations.") And earlier, when the verse was revealed:

"Fasabbih... al-'azim" ("So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty"), he instructed that it be recited in bowing (ruku'). Hence "Subhana Rabbiya al-'Azim" began to be recited in ruku'. Thus the tasbih of ruku' and sujud is a living tasbih, not merely lifeless words; just as the body of a living thing is warm with life and vitality, such tasbih is desired in salah, so that through this tasbih the command of Allah is directly fulfilled, or, in other words, the permission of Allah is fulfilled. For Allah's granting His servants permission to praise Him is also an act of His grace and bounty, because through it a human being is granted permission to draw near to Allah in accordance with the limit of his conception. A person can praise Allah, and speak of His Being and attributes, only according to his limited conception. And it is a form of Allah's grace and generosity that He makes His servants know His Being through His attributes, within limits within which they can conceive the knowledge of Him. Whatever form of permission Allah gives His servants to reach His Being, it is a form of grace upon them.

"Sabbih isma... fahda" (87:1–3): "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and proportioned, who measured out and then guided." That is, He created everything and created it in a most fitting form, and perfected every aspect of that creation, to such a degree that no one can say that any of its features is unsuitable for it. Allah measured out (qaddara) so that for everything He fixed its appointed function, and He also explained to it its purpose of creation and the method of fulfilling that purpose. Everything was taught in a wondrous inspired manner. He also gave to everything, by way of inspiration, the awareness of what it needs for its appointed life.

This is a great truth, and in whatever thing of this universe one analyses, this truth is present. In every thing of this vast and wide universe, whether large or small, important or insignificant, there is harmony (taswiyah) and proportion in its creation. Every thing is perfect in its creation, every thing has a purpose of creation, and that purpose is its taqdir (measure), and Allah has provided for every thing a most easy method of carrying out its purpose of existence. In short, every creature of Allah is complete and proportioned, and every thing performs its individual duty.

For example, a single atom maintains within itself, between its proton and the electric motion of its electrons, the same balance as a galaxy maintains between its sun and the stars that are subject to it. An atom fulfils its purpose and duty in the same way as a galaxy does; both are seen to know their purpose and the method of attaining it.

A single cell is a complete creation, and within it there is the full capacity to fulfil its purpose of creation, and it fulfils its purpose in the same way as any high compound and complex creature does.

Then there are different creatures at intermediate levels between a single atom and a galaxy. Just as between a single cell and the most complex creatures there are various levels of living beings and their organisation. In the creation of every level and every organisation there is perfection and harmony, and for each there are individual duties and collective purposes. The hand of power makes them carry out this work in an inspired manner, and this profound truth, namely the work of creation and proportioning, is a witness that is just (shahid 'adl) upon the whole universe.

The human heart can attain this truth provided it is ready to derive the indications of this universe and reflects upon the existents of the universe with an open heart. Whatever the level of a person's acquired knowledge, and whether he is a member of an advanced society or of a backward society, he can derive these inspired indications from the things of the universe, provided the windows of his heart and mind are also ready to receive these indications and are open, and provided some strings of reason and wisdom are fit to respond with melody to the plectrum of truth.

After this come the observation of the universe and various sciences, and the human being, in the study of nature, receives from the first glance an inspiration, and all observations confirm it. Some people, through observing the universe, have gathered such indications as lift the veil from the face of the collective truth hidden within this universe.

Mr. Chrissie Morrison, president of the Academy of Scientific Sciences of New York, records his observations in his book "Man Does Not Stand Alone" as follows:

"Birds have a faculty of returning home. A certain sparrow that builds its nest on doorways migrates south in the autumn season and returns to the same place in the spring of the following year. In the month of September most of the birds of America travel south, and flying over seas and deserts they cover thousands of miles, and never lose their way. And homing pigeons travel long distances in cages, and when they are released with a message they circle for a while in bewilderment, and after that they fly straight towards their homeland, and never stray from the path. If a honeybee goes somewhere and the traces of its path are erased by some storm, it still does not lose its way and comes straight back to the hive. However, in man this instinct is weak, and man makes up for this deficiency through his instruments and reason. Tiny insects also have extremely small and microscopic eyes, and these are most perfect eyes. The eyes of hawks and eagles and the like are like binoculars; the human eye cannot compete with them. This deficiency too has been made up by human reason and experience. Thus through these binoculars man sees the stars, and he has increased the sharpness of human vision a million-fold for seeing them. Moreover, man has invented such microscopes through which he sees bacteria and other creatures that are not visible to the eye."

"Now just let your old horse loose on the road. However dark it may be, it will not lose its way. It can see even in deep darkness, though perhaps not very clearly. It can see the temperature on the road and on both sides of it. Its eyes perceive this temperature through infrared rays. The owl can see a warm mouse moving beneath cold grass even when it is pitch dark, and humans have turned the dark night into day through the lights of electric bulbs."

"The world of honeybees is also wondrous. The worker bees construct different kinds of chambers in the hive. These are used for rearing. Small chambers are used for the workers and large chambers for the males, and special chambers are prepared for the queen. The queen, when she lays an unfertilised egg, places it in the chamber of the males, and when she lays a fertilised egg, she places it in the chamber in which the female worker bees are, who will in time become queen bees; and the worker bees, which are labourers, when they have performed the task of producing offspring for a long time, are replaced. These worker bees also perform the task of preparing food for the young. They chew honey and pollen and make them digestible, and when the sex of the young becomes manifest, they cease the process of preparing food in the above-mentioned manner. After this they are given honey and pollen-dust, and among the young those females who are trained in this manner later become worker bees."

As for the female bees that are in the cells of the queen bees, the feeding of them with honey and pollen-dust, made digestible in the initial stage, continues, and those female bees who are treated in this way later become queen bees. Only this queen lays eggs that are fertilised. In accordance with this technology, the young that are born require special kinds of cells, a special kind of egg, and a special kind of food. And the effect of the change in food is also wondrous. For this technology, the bees must have needed a long period of waiting, during which they distinguished these principles, applied them, and learned the effects of food, and applied collectively what was necessary for their existence. When the bees began their collective life, they must have then learned these principles, because for the existence of the bee and the preservation of its life these principles did not need to be discovered. Therefore it appears that the honeybee has researched the effects of food more than man has."

(The author, immersed in Western thought, is not prepared to accept that when Allah created the bee He taught it all this. Darwin's philosophy of evolution sits upon their minds, whereas the Qur'an clearly says: "And He taught Adam the names, all of them" — Allah taught Adam all the names; in the same way Allah gave the bee all its basic instruction. (Translator.))

"The dog has been given an additional nose through which it smells every animal that has passed along a path. Human olfactory power is weak in comparison with dogs, and to this day man has not invented any instrument that develops his sense of smell. Yet even this weak sense of smell of ours perceives such tiny particles as can be seen only through a microscope."

Most animals hear sounds that cannot cause vibration in the eardrums of our ears, because these are too subtle and fine for the limit of our hearing. Man has invented such instruments that he can hear even the sound of the wings of a fly flying miles away, as though it were sitting on the eardrum of his ear. By such instruments the sound of the speed of the sun's rays is also being recorded."

"There is a kind of water spider which builds a nest under water like a balloon. It is made of spider silk, and it is fastened to something beneath the water. Then this spider carries bubbles of water with the hairs of its body and takes them and attaches them to the nest, until a barrier of air bubbles forms around the nest. After that it lays its young inside the nest so that they remain safe from the storm of air. In the structure of this nest there is, on the one hand, the process of fine weaving, and after that, deep engineering and a profound understanding of aeronautics."

Salmon, which are small fish, spend several years roaming the sea, and then return to the river where they were born. What is the force that guides them back to their birthplace? If one, while heading toward its birthplace, enters a wrong river, it immediately knows that this river is not its birthplace. So it moves within the river and, swimming against the current, reaches its destination.

The case of sea serpents is very strange, and their story is the opposite of the salmon's. When the life of this creature of God is complete, it travels from various ponds and rivers toward the deep seas. If they are in Europe, they cover thousands of miles and head to the depths of South Bermuda. There they lay eggs and die. Their offspring, when born, know only that they are in very deep waters. Yet these young follow the same route to the shore that their mother took when she came from the shore to the water. From the shore they then go to some river, canal, pool or pond. Thus every kind of water is suitable for sea serpents, because they have seen and faced great waves, storms and ocean turbulence. They travel along the coasts, and when they are fully grown, some hidden law compels them to return and go back to the deep seas. The question is: where does this urge arise within them? It has never happened that a hunter or fisherman caught an American sea serpent in European seas, or that a European serpent came into the net of an American fisherman. Because the European sea serpent must travel a long distance to the deep seas, nature gave it a long life of one year, or even more, so that it could reach its destined goal before dying, since the European sea serpent must cover a greater distance than the American one. Just look: what atoms and what molecules are these? When sea serpents gather in the form of fish, how does such a power of will arise within them that makes them undertake such distant journeys?

When the female moth enters through a ventilator of your home, carried by the wind, she sends a signal to her male, however far he may be. Sometimes he is very far away. He receives that signal and responds to it. No matter how hard a human tries to mislead it, it is impossible for it to make a mistake. Is there a radio station with them, or does that male have a radio or machine that receives signals from her? Let alone an aerial, is there an ether through which she creates vibrations? Our telephones and radios are rapid communication devices, but they connect one place to another through wires. In this way, this moth is superior to us.

Plants, without knowledge or intention, make use of many things to maintain their existence. For example, insects carry pollen to them; the wind does the same work; wild animals and birds also do this work, scattering their pollen and seeds. In the end, these plants also ensnared humans in their net. Humans gave beauty to nature, and nature gave them their reward. But humans also do not stop at any limit. Humans believe in *hal min mazid* (is there more?). They plowed, sowed seed, harvested, filled storehouses, then developed the crops, pruned branches and arranged food supplies. If they gave up this work, they would die of hunger, civilization and culture would end, and humanity would return to the Stone Age.

In many water creatures, such as the prawn, if one of its arms is cut off, it knows that a part of its body has been lost. Its cells and genes begin to rebuild that organ, and when the organ is complete, the cells stop this work and know that their duty has ended.

Water worms that have many legs, when they are split into two pieces, complete themselves using one of the pieces. If you cut off the head of this worm, it creates a second head.

We can heal wounds, but our surgeons still do not know how to activate cells so that they can create a new arm, or produce flesh, nails and nerves, if that were possible.

And there is another marvel: if a cell divides into two complete parts in its early days, two complete animals are produced from it. We see that twins are alike in appearance. This can be explained by the fact that in the early stage of pregnancy the cell divided, and from this it is also understood that in the early stage the cell is a complete individual, and similarly an individual exists in every cell.

In another chapter, this same author writes:

"The brown seed of the oak tree falls to the ground. Its brown shell protects it, and it tumbles and gets lodged in a crack in the earth. In the spring season its inner germ awakens. It breaks open that shell and draws nourishment from the kernel that has been stored inside the shell, within which lie its hereditary genes. Its roots go into the earth. You see that this plant emerges, becomes a small tree, and then becomes a complete tree. It contains many millions of genes. Until it resembles, in its roots, shell, fruit, trunk and branches, the tree from which that seed came. Millions of years ago, the oak tree that came into being produced fruits that to this day maintain the arrangement of their particles in the same way as the first oak fruit did."

This same author, in a third chapter, writes: "Every cell that is produced in a living creature is obliged to adapt itself so that it becomes a part of flesh or a part of skin, and either perishes, or becomes the shine of a tooth, or becomes the liquid matter of the eye, or becomes the nose and ears. Every cell adapts itself into a form so that it fully performs its designated duty. It is extremely difficult for anyone to determine which cell belongs to the right hand or the left hand. But by nature it is determined that this cell belongs to the right ear and that cell to the left ear. In short, thousands of cells are driven so that they do the right work, at the right time and in the right place."

In a fourth chapter, this person says: "Among various kinds of creatures, some perform works that reflect the highest level of wisdom, whose explanation we cannot provide. For example, the wasp hunts the grasshopper. It digs a pit in the earth and buries it in a suitable place. While hunting, it stings the grasshopper at such a specific point that it becomes unconscious, yet its flesh remains intact and alive. Now the female wasp lays her eggs at a fixed place near it. Perhaps she does not even know that when her young are born they will eat the flesh of this grasshopper, but they will not kill it, because this flesh is their food, and if the flesh spoiled it would become poisonous. Surely the wasp must have begun this work from the beginning, and she must always repeat it, otherwise the existence of wasps would have ended from the world. Science has no explanation that could state the cause of this continuous action of the wasps, and it is also not possible that the wasps do this work merely by chance, because the female wasp fills the pit she has dug in the earth and goes away and dies. Neither did her ancestors know why she does this, nor does she know or observe what her young will face afterward. Rather, the wasp does not even know that there is anything coming after her that she would call her child. It does not even know that she does this work for the protection of the species."

Among ants, some have the duty of gathering creatures to supply food to their colony during the winter season. Then they establish a store where this food is ground and kept. Then some ants are such that nature has given them grinding jaws. Their work is only to grind the food. When winter comes and all the grain has been ground, its supply is arranged so that the greatest possible number of ants benefit, so that the supply can continue. Now, since more grinding ants will be born in the next generation, the army of ants attacks those grinding ants and kills them. Perhaps their conscience is satisfied that they have eaten their share of food during the grinding, since they must have benefited from that opportunity.

Some ants are such that their instinct or their intelligence moves them to create gardens of food. These ants capture small insects and insects found on the shells of plants. These insects serve them like cows and goats. From these insects the ants take a liquid like honey, which serves as food for the ants.

Ants also enslave some other ants. When they build their nests, they cut leaves to a suitable size. When worker ants hold these leaves from one side and place them in position, they also make use of the young ants that are still in their developmental stage, using their silky material to join the leaves. Thus that young ant is deprived of building a nest for itself, yet it has already performed a useful task for its kind. The question is: how does the ability to do this work arise in the particles from which an ant is made? There is no doubt that there is a Creator who guided them to act in this way."

(Quotations end.)

There is no doubt that there is a Creator who gave guidance to all His creatures, whether they are large or small, and this is the same Creator who is ﴿the Most High…﴾ and guided (87:1–3): ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and proportioned, who determined and then guided.﴾

What we have quoted above are observations on only a small part of the reality, which humans have recorded regarding plants, insects, birds and other animals. But beyond this there are more worlds of knowledge and observation, and what is known to us is only a very small portion of the meaning and significance of this statement of God.

﴿Who created and proportioned, who determined and then guided﴾ (87:2–3). This observable universe, of which we know only a small part, has beyond it hidden worlds of the unseen. We have been given only a little knowledge according to our human capacities. These are a few indications that God has provided for our limited power of perception.

After presenting a broad page of this great universe and creating within its valleys the echo of God's glorification and praise, in order to complete this great tasbih of God, here a reference is made to the world of plants, and within this reference there is a world of meanings.

﴿And who brought forth the pasture, then made it dark stubble﴾ (87:4–5). *Al-mar'a* is applied to everything that grows from the earth, because every growing thing is food for some creature. Therefore, the meaning of *mar'a* here is far broader than saying that something is *mar'a* only if it is grazed by our livestock. God created the earth and, for every creature that moves upon this earth, provided its food within it, whether that creature moves on the earth, hides within it, or flies in its skies.

Plants are first green, then they wither and become dark. Sometimes they are fit for food while still green, and sometimes they ripen and become dark, and then they serve as food. Even in the intermediate state they serve as some kind of food. In any case, every state of plants becomes food for some creature, according to God's creation and proportioning.

By presenting the scene of plant life, a sign is given here that just as every plant ends up as rubbish, so every living creature also reaches its end in this world. This is also a sign pointing to this worldly life and the life of the Hereafter: that worldly life, like plants, is destined to end, while the life of the Hereafter remains and is everlasting. This comes later:

﴿But you prefer the worldly life, while the Hereafter is better and more lasting﴾ (87:16–17). Worldly life is like a field that ends and becomes rubbish, while the Hereafter is enduring and everlasting.

Through this closing passage, the pages of this great universe are spread out far and wide, and the matters mentioned are appropriate to the realities that come in this surah. This universe harmonizes with them, and these realities are woven into the universe. It is a very broad and expansive framework. If one studies deeply, the themes of this section of the Qur'an are presented within a vast cosmic scope. This cosmic scope harmonizes with the atmosphere of this portion and with its indications and themes.

God created the earth and, for every creature that moves upon this earth, provided its food within it, whether that creature moves on the earth, hides within it, or flies in its skies.

Through this closing passage, the pages of this great universe are spread out far and wide, and the matters mentioned are appropriate to the realities that come in this surah. This universe harmonizes with them, and these realities are woven into the universe. It is a very broad and expansive framework. If one studies deeply, the themes of this section of the Qur'an are presented within a vast cosmic scope. This cosmic scope harmonizes with the atmosphere of this portion and with its indications and themes.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 87, verses 1–5 (part 1 of 2):

The opening of the surah begins with a very gentle and long-drawn cadence; through this lengthened tone a pleasant and fragrant sound of tasbih (glorification) is spread through the atmosphere. After this comes the command to glorify, and then the attributes that have been brought after the glorification.

"Sabbih isma..." to "ahwa" (87:1–5): "(O Prophet!) Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and proportioned, who measured out and then guided, who brought forth the pasture and then made it dark, withered rubbish." The purpose is that through this tasbih the sound of glorification should echo in every corner and expanse of this whole universe, and the whole universe should appear as a place of worship (ma'bad), and, alongside being a place of worship, the whole universe should also become an exhibition hall of the products of the Creator's power.

"Alladhi... fahda" (87:3): "who created and proportioned, who measured out and then guided."

What are the meanings of tasbih? Keeping the supremacy of Allah in mind, regarding Allah as free from every defect, keeping the attributes of Allah's beautiful names (asma' al-husna) present in the mind, and keeping one's taste, intuition, heart and consciousness illuminated by the light, brightness and radiance of these things: this is what tasbih is called. Merely reciting "Subhan Allah" with the tongue is not called tasbih.

"Sabbih... al-a'la" (87:1): "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High." These words bring upon human intuition and consciousness a particular state. This intuitive state is of such a kind that its expression is not possible in words. It is indeed an intuitive and experiential matter, and it points to a kind of life that is connected with the remembrance of certain meanings and certain attributes, not with the rote memorization of words.

What are these meanings and attributes? The first attribute is the attribute of rububiyyah (lordship), and the second is that of al-a'la (the Most High). Rabb means nurturer, supervisor and sustainer. The shadows and reflections of these attributes are in harmony with the atmosphere of this surah and with the glad tidings expressed within it, especially with its gentle manner. The attribute al-a'la brings before the screen of consciousness images through which loftiness, supremacy, and a limitless and boundless horizon are expressed. The human soul glorifies (tasbih) far into the distance, and through this concept of loftiness, tasbih acquires a connection with purity and greatness, and tasbih, in terms of its basic elements, is the name of the concept of the loftiness of the Lord.

The initial address is clearly to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it is a direct address to him from Allah. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite this command of his Lord, "Sabbih" ("glorify"), he would act upon this command before reading the following verses, and would say: "Subhana Rabbiya al-a'la" ("I glorify my Lord, the Most High"). Thus the command and the response to the command, or the fulfilment of the command, would take place, the obedience to the command would be accomplished, and there would be a supplication and a question-and-answer with Allah. Because the Messenger stood before his Lord, he was receiving this speech directly from the Lord, and in that state of connection and closeness he would give the response. When these verses were revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) instructed the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) to recite this tasbih in prostration. (Ij'alūhā fī sujūdikum – "Make it in your prostrations.") And earlier, when the verse was revealed:

"Fasabbih... al-'azim" ("So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty"), he instructed that it be recited in bowing (ruku'). Hence "Subhana Rabbiya al-'Azim" began to be recited in ruku'. Thus the tasbih of ruku' and sujud is a living tasbih, not merely lifeless words; just as the body of a living thing is warm with life and vitality, such tasbih is desired in salah, so that through this tasbih the command of Allah is directly fulfilled, or, in other words, the permission of Allah is fulfilled. For Allah's granting His servants permission to praise Him is also an act of His grace and bounty, because through it a human being is granted permission to draw near to Allah in accordance with the limit of his conception. A person can praise Allah, and speak of His Being and attributes, only according to his limited conception. And it is a form of Allah's grace and generosity that He makes His servants know His Being through His attributes, within limits within which they can conceive the knowledge of Him. Whatever form of permission Allah gives His servants to reach His Being, it is a form of grace upon them.

"Sabbih isma... fahda" (87:1–3): "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and proportioned, who measured out and then guided." That is, He created everything and created it in a most fitting form, and perfected every aspect of that creation, to such a degree that no one can say that any of its features is unsuitable for it. Allah measured out (qaddara) so that for everything He fixed its appointed function, and He also explained to it its purpose of creation and the method of fulfilling that purpose. Everything was taught in a wondrous inspired manner. He also gave to everything, by way of inspiration, the awareness of what it needs for its appointed life.

This is a great truth, and in whatever thing of this universe one analyses, this truth is present. In every thing of this vast and wide universe, whether large or small, important or insignificant, there is harmony (taswiyah) and proportion in its creation. Every thing is perfect in its creation, every thing has a purpose of creation, and that purpose is its taqdir (measure), and Allah has provided for every thing a most easy method of carrying out its purpose of existence. In short, every creature of Allah is complete and proportioned, and every thing performs its individual duty.

For example, a single atom maintains within itself, between its proton and the electric motion of its electrons, the same balance as a galaxy maintains between its sun and the stars that are subject to it. An atom fulfils its purpose and duty in the same way as a galaxy does; both are seen to know their purpose and the method of attaining it.

A single cell is a complete creation, and within it there is the full capacity to fulfil its purpose of creation, and it fulfils its purpose in the same way as any high compound and complex creature does.

Then there are different creatures at intermediate levels between a single atom and a galaxy. Just as between a single cell and the most complex creatures there are various levels of living beings and their organisation. In the creation of every level and every organisation there is perfection and harmony, and for each there are individual duties and collective purposes. The hand of power makes them carry out this work in an inspired manner, and this profound truth, namely the work of creation and proportioning, is a witness that is just (shahid 'adl) upon the whole universe.

The human heart can attain this truth provided it is ready to derive the indications of this universe and reflects upon the existents of the universe with an open heart. Whatever the level of a person's acquired knowledge, and whether he is a member of an advanced society or of a backward society, he can derive these inspired indications from the things of the universe, provided the windows of his heart and mind are also ready to receive these indications and are open, and provided some strings of reason and wisdom are fit to respond with melody to the plectrum of truth.

After this come the observation of the universe and various sciences, and the human being, in the study of nature, receives from the first glance an inspiration, and all observations confirm it. Some people, through observing the universe, have gathered such indications as lift the veil from the face of the collective truth hidden within this universe.

You see that this plant emerges, becomes a small tree, and then becomes a complete tree. It contains many millions of genes. Millions of years ago, the oak tree that came into being produced fruits that to this day maintain the arrangement of their particles in the same way as the first oak fruit did."

This same author, in a third chapter, writes: "Every cell that is produced in a living creature is obliged to adapt itself so that it becomes a part of flesh or a part of skin, and either perishes, or becomes the shine of a tooth, or becomes the liquid matter of the eye, or becomes the nose and ears. Every cell adapts itself into a form so that it fully performs its designated duty. It is extremely difficult for anyone to determine which cell belongs to the right hand or the left hand. For example, the wasp hunts the grasshopper. It digs a pit in the earth and buries it in a suitable place. While hunting, it stings the grasshopper at such a specific point that it becomes unconscious, yet its flesh remains intact and alive. Now the female wasp lays her eggs at a fixed place near it. Among ants, some have the duty of gathering creatures to supply food to their colony during the winter season. Then they establish a store where this food is ground and kept. Then some ants are such that nature has given them grinding jaws. Their work is only to grind the food. When winter comes and all the grain has been ground, its supply is arranged so that the greatest possible number of ants benefit, so that the supply can continue. Now, since more grinding ants will be born in the next generation, the army of ants attacks those grinding ants and kills them. Perhaps their conscience is satisfied that they have eaten their share of food during the grinding, since they must have benefited from that opportunity.

Some ants are such that their instinct or their intelligence moves them to create gardens of food. These ants capture small insects and insects found on the shells of plants. These insects serve them like cows and goats. From these insects the ants take a liquid like honey, which serves as food for the ants.

There is no doubt that there is a Creator who gave guidance to all His creatures, whether they are large or small, and this is the same Creator who is ﴿the Most High…﴾ and guided (87:1–3): ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and proportioned, who determined and then guided.﴾

What we have quoted above are observations on only a small part of the reality, which humans have recorded regarding plants, insects, birds and other animals. But beyond this there are more worlds of knowledge and observation, and what is known to us is only a very small portion of the meaning and significance of this statement of God.

﴿Who created and proportioned, who determined and then guided﴾ (87:2–3). This observable universe, of which we know only a small part, has beyond it hidden worlds of the unseen. We have been given only a little knowledge according to our human capacities. These are a few indications that God has provided for our limited power of perception.

After presenting a broad page of this great universe and creating within its valleys the echo of God's glorification and praise, in order to complete this great tasbih of God, here a reference is made to the world of plants, and within this reference there is a world of meanings.

﴿And who brought forth the pasture, then made it dark stubble﴾ (87:4–5). *Al-mar'a* is applied to everything that grows from the earth, because every growing thing is food for some creature. Therefore, the meaning of *mar'a* here is far broader than saying that something is *mar'a* only if it is grazed by our livestock. God created the earth and, for every creature that moves upon this earth, provided its food within it, whether that creature moves on the earth, hides within it, or flies in its skies.

Plants are first green, then they wither and become dark. Sometimes they are fit for food while still green, and sometimes they ripen and become dark, and then they serve as food. Even in the intermediate state they serve as some kind of food. In any case, every state of plants becomes food for some creature, according to God's creation and proportioning.

By presenting the scene of plant life, a sign is given here that just as every plant ends up as rubbish, so every living creature also reaches its end in this world. This is also a sign pointing to this worldly life and the life of the Hereafter: that worldly life, like plants, is destined to end, while the life of the Hereafter remains and is everlasting. This comes later:

Through this closing passage, the pages of this great universe are spread out far and wide, and the matters mentioned are appropriate to the realities that come in this surah. This universe harmonizes with them, and these realities are woven into the universe. It is a very broad and expansive framework. If one studies deeply, the themes of this section of the Qur'an are presented within a vast cosmic scope. This cosmic scope harmonizes with the atmosphere of this portion and with its indications and themes.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 87, verses 1–5 (part 1 of 2):

The opening of the surah begins with a very gentle and long-drawn cadence; through this lengthened tone a pleasant and fragrant sound of tasbih (glorification) is spread through the atmosphere. After this comes the command to glorify, and then the attributes that have been brought after the glorification.

"Sabbih isma..." to "ahwa" (87:1–5): "(O Prophet!) Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and proportioned, who measured out and then guided, who brought forth the pasture and then made it dark, withered rubbish." The purpose is that through this tasbih the sound of glorification should echo in every corner and expanse of this whole universe, and the whole universe should appear as a place of worship (ma'bad), and, alongside being a place of worship, the whole universe should also become an exhibition hall of the products of the Creator's power.

"Alladhi... fahda" (87:3): "who created and proportioned, who measured out and then guided."

What are the meanings of tasbih? Keeping the supremacy of Allah in mind, regarding Allah as free from every defect, keeping the attributes of Allah's beautiful names (asma' al-husna) present in the mind, and keeping one's taste, intuition, heart and consciousness illuminated by the light, brightness and radiance of these things: this is what tasbih is called. Merely reciting "Subhan Allah" with the tongue is not called tasbih.

"Sabbih... al-a'la" (87:1): "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High." These words bring upon human intuition and consciousness a particular state. This intuitive state is of such a kind that its expression is not possible in words. It is indeed an intuitive and experiential matter, and it points to a kind of life that is connected with the remembrance of certain meanings and certain attributes, not with the rote memorization of words.

What are these meanings and attributes? The first attribute is the attribute of rububiyyah (lordship), and the second is that of al-a'la (the Most High). Rabb means nurturer, supervisor and sustainer. The shadows and reflections of these attributes are in harmony with the atmosphere of this surah and with the glad tidings expressed within it, especially with its gentle manner. The attribute al-a'la brings before the screen of consciousness images through which loftiness, supremacy, and a limitless and boundless horizon are expressed. The human soul glorifies (tasbih) far into the distance, and through this concept of loftiness, tasbih acquires a connection with purity and greatness, and tasbih, in terms of its basic elements, is the name of the concept of the loftiness of the Lord.

The initial address is clearly to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it is a direct address to him from Allah. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite this command of his Lord, "Sabbih" ("glorify"), he would act upon this command before reading the following verses, and would say: "Subhana Rabbiya al-a'la" ("I glorify my Lord, the Most High"). Thus the command and the response to the command, or the fulfilment of the command, would take place, the obedience to the command would be accomplished, and there would be a supplication and a question-and-answer with Allah. Because the Messenger stood before his Lord, he was receiving this speech directly from the Lord, and in that state of connection and closeness he would give the response. When these verses were revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) instructed the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) to recite this tasbih in prostration. (Ij'alūhā fī sujūdikum – "Make it in your prostrations.") And earlier, when the verse was revealed:

"Fasabbih... al-'azim" ("So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty"), he instructed that it be recited in bowing (ruku'). Hence "Subhana Rabbiya al-'Azim" began to be recited in ruku'. Thus the tasbih of ruku' and sujud is a living tasbih, not merely lifeless words; just as the body of a living thing is warm with life and vitality, such tasbih is desired in salah, so that through this tasbih the command of Allah is directly fulfilled, or, in other words, the permission of Allah is fulfilled. For Allah's granting His servants permission to praise Him is also an act of His grace and bounty, because through it a human being is granted permission to draw near to Allah in accordance with the limit of his conception. A person can praise Allah, and speak of His Being and attributes, only according to his limited conception. And it is a form of Allah's grace and generosity that He makes His servants know His Being through His attributes, within limits within which they can conceive the knowledge of Him. Whatever form of permission Allah gives His servants to reach His Being, it is a form of grace upon them.

"Sabbih isma... fahda" (87:1–3): "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and proportioned, who measured out and then guided." That is, He created everything and created it in a most fitting form, and perfected every aspect of that creation, to such a degree that no one can say that any of its features is unsuitable for it. Allah measured out (qaddara) so that for everything He fixed its appointed function, and He also explained to it its purpose of creation and the method of fulfilling that purpose. Everything was taught in a wondrous inspired manner. He also gave to everything, by way of inspiration, the awareness of what it needs for its appointed life.

This is a great truth, and in whatever thing of this universe one analyses, this truth is present. In every thing of this vast and wide universe, whether large or small, important or insignificant, there is harmony (taswiyah) and proportion in its creation. Every thing is perfect in its creation, every thing has a purpose of creation, and that purpose is its taqdir (measure), and Allah has provided for every thing a most easy method of carrying out its purpose of existence. In short, every creature of Allah is complete and proportioned, and every thing performs its individual duty.

For example, a single atom maintains within itself, between its proton and the electric motion of its electrons, the same balance as a galaxy maintains between its sun and the stars that are subject to it. An atom fulfils its purpose and duty in the same way as a galaxy does; both are seen to know their purpose and the method of attaining it.

A single cell is a complete creation, and within it there is the full capacity to fulfil its purpose of creation, and it fulfils its purpose in the same way as any high compound and complex creature does.

Then there are different creatures at intermediate levels between a single atom and a galaxy. Just as between a single cell and the most complex creatures there are various levels of living beings and their organisation. In the creation of every level and every organisation there is perfection and harmony, and for each there are individual duties and collective purposes. The hand of power makes them carry out this work in an inspired manner, and this profound truth, namely the work of creation and proportioning, is a witness that is just (shahid 'adl) upon the whole universe.

The human heart can attain this truth provided it is ready to derive the indications of this universe and reflects upon the existents of the universe with an open heart. Whatever the level of a person's acquired knowledge, and whether he is a member of an advanced society or of a backward society, he can derive these inspired indications from the things of the universe, provided the windows of his heart and mind are also ready to receive these indications and are open, and provided some strings of reason and wisdom are fit to respond with melody to the plectrum of truth.

After this come the observation of the universe and various sciences, and the human being, in the study of nature, receives from the first glance an inspiration, and all observations confirm it. Some people, through observing the universe, have gathered such indications as lift the veil from the face of the collective truth hidden within this universe.

Mr. Chrissie Morrison, president of the Academy of Scientific Sciences of New York, records his observations in his book "Man Does Not Stand Alone" as follows:

"Birds have a faculty of returning home. A certain sparrow that builds its nest on doorways migrates south in the autumn season and returns to the same place in the spring of the following year. And homing pigeons travel long distances in cages, and when they are released with a message they circle for a while in bewilderment, and after that they fly straight towards their homeland, and never stray from the path. If a honeybee goes somewhere and the traces of its path are erased by some storm, it still does not lose its way and comes straight back to the hive. However, in man this instinct is weak, and man makes up for this deficiency through his instruments and reason. Tiny insects also have extremely small and microscopic eyes, and these are most perfect eyes. The eyes of hawks and eagles and the like are like binoculars; the human eye cannot compete with them. This deficiency too has been made up by human reason and experience. Thus through these binoculars man sees the stars, and he has increased the sharpness of human vision a million-fold for seeing them. Moreover, man has invented such microscopes through which he sees bacteria and other creatures that are not visible to the eye."

"Now just let your old horse loose on the road. However dark it may be, it will not lose its way. It can see even in deep darkness, though perhaps not very clearly. It can see the temperature on the road and on both sides of it. Its eyes perceive this temperature through infrared rays. These worker bees also perform the task of preparing food for the young. They chew honey and pollen and make them digestible, and when the sex of the young becomes manifest, they cease the process of preparing food in the above-mentioned manner. After this they are given honey and pollen-dust, and among the young those females who are trained in this manner later become worker bees."

As for the female bees that are in the cells of the queen bees, the feeding of them with honey and pollen-dust, made digestible in the initial stage, continues, and those female bees who are treated in this way later become queen bees. Only this queen lays eggs that are fertilised. In accordance with this technology, the young that are born require special kinds of cells, a special kind of egg, and a special kind of food. And the effect of the change in food is also wondrous. For this technology, the bees must have needed a long period of waiting, during which they distinguished these principles, applied them, and learned the effects of food, and applied collectively what was necessary for their existence. When the bees began their collective life, they must have then learned these principles, because for the existence of the bee and the preservation of its life these principles did not need to be discovered. Therefore it appears that the honeybee has researched the effects of food more than man has."

(The author, immersed in Western thought, is not prepared to accept that when Allah created the bee He taught it all this. Darwin's philosophy of evolution sits upon their minds, whereas the Qur'an clearly says: "And He taught Adam the names, all of them" — Allah taught Adam all the names; in the same way Allah gave the bee all its basic instruction. "The dog has been given an additional nose through which it smells every animal that has passed along a path. Most animals hear sounds that cannot cause vibration in the eardrums of our ears, because these are too subtle and fine for the limit of our hearing. Man has invented such instruments that he can hear even the sound of the wings of a fly flying miles away, as though it were sitting on the eardrum of his ear. By such instruments the sound of the speed of the sun's rays is also being recorded."

Then this spider carries bubbles of water with the hairs of its body and takes them and attaches them to the nest, until a barrier of air bubbles forms around the nest. After that it lays its young inside the nest so that they remain safe from the storm of air. In the structure of this nest there is, on the one hand, the process of fine weaving, and after that, deep engineering and a profound understanding of aeronautics."

Salmon, which are small fish, spend several years roaming the sea, and then return to the river where they were born. What is the force that guides them back to their birthplace? If one, while heading toward its birthplace, enters a wrong river, it immediately knows that this river is not its birthplace. So it moves within the river and, swimming against the current, reaches its destination.

Water worms that have many legs, when they are split into two pieces, complete themselves using one of the pieces. If you cut off the head of this worm, it creates a second head.
