"Sabbih... al-a'la" (87:1): "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High." These words bring upon human intuition and consciousness a particular state. This intuitive state is of such a kind that its expression is not possible in words. It is indeed an intuitive and experiential matter, and it points to a kind of life that is connected with the remembrance of certain meanings and certain attributes, not with the rote memorization of words.

What are these meanings and attributes? The first attribute is the attribute of rububiyyah (lordship), and the second is that of al-a'la (the Most High). Rabb means nurturer, supervisor and sustainer. The shadows and reflections of these attributes are in harmony with the atmosphere of this surah and with the glad tidings expressed within it, especially with its gentle manner. The attribute al-a'la brings before the screen of consciousness images through which loftiness, supremacy, and a limitless and boundless horizon are expressed. The human soul glorifies (tasbih) far into the distance, and through this concept of loftiness, tasbih acquires a connection with purity and greatness, and tasbih, in terms of its basic elements, is the name of the concept of the loftiness of the Lord.

The initial address is clearly to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it is a direct address to him from Allah. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite this command of his Lord, "Sabbih" ("glorify"), he would act upon this command before reading the following verses, and would say: "Subhana Rabbiya al-a'la" ("I glorify my Lord, the Most High"). Thus the command and the response to the command, or the fulfilment of the command, would take place, the obedience to the command would be accomplished, and there would be a supplication and a question-and-answer with Allah. Because the Messenger stood before his Lord, he was receiving this speech directly from the Lord, and in that state of connection and closeness he would give the response. When these verses were revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) instructed the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) to recite this tasbih in prostration. (Ij'alūhā fī sujūdikum – "Make it in your prostrations.") And earlier, when the verse was revealed:

"Fasabbih... al-'azim" ("So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty"), he instructed that it be recited in bowing (ruku'). Hence "Subhana Rabbiya al-'Azim" began to be recited in ruku'. Thus the tasbih of ruku' and sujud is a living tasbih, not merely lifeless words; just as the body of a living thing is warm with life and vitality, such tasbih is desired in salah, so that through this tasbih the command of Allah is directly fulfilled, or, in other words, the permission of Allah is fulfilled. For Allah's granting His servants permission to praise Him is also an act of His grace and bounty, because through it a human being is granted permission to draw near to Allah in accordance with the limit of his conception. A person can praise Allah, and speak of His Being and attributes, only according to his limited conception. And it is a form of Allah's grace and generosity that He makes His servants know His Being through His attributes, within limits within which they can conceive the knowledge of Him. Whatever form of permission Allah gives His servants to reach His Being, it is a form of grace upon them.

"Sabbih isma... fahda" (87:1–3): "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and proportioned, who measured out and then guided." That is, He created everything and created it in a most fitting form, and perfected every aspect of that creation, to such a degree that no one can say that any of its features is unsuitable for it. Allah measured out (qaddara) so that for everything He fixed its appointed function, and He also explained to it its purpose of creation and the method of fulfilling that purpose. Everything was taught in a wondrous inspired manner. He also gave to everything, by way of inspiration, the awareness of what it needs for its appointed life.

This is a great truth, and in whatever thing of this universe one analyses, this truth is present. In every thing of this vast and wide universe, whether large or small, important or insignificant, there is harmony (taswiyah) and proportion in its creation. Every thing is perfect in its creation, every thing has a purpose of creation, and that purpose is its taqdir (measure), and Allah has provided for every thing a most easy method of carrying out its purpose of existence. In short, every creature of Allah is complete and proportioned, and every thing performs its individual duty.

For example, a single atom maintains within itself, between its proton and the electric motion of its electrons, the same balance as a galaxy maintains between its sun and the stars that are subject to it. An atom fulfils its purpose and duty in the same way as a galaxy does; both are seen to know their purpose and the method of attaining it.

A single cell is a complete creation, and within it there is the full capacity to fulfil its purpose of creation, and it fulfils its purpose in the same way as any high compound and complex creature does.

Then there are different creatures at intermediate levels between a single atom and a galaxy. Just as between a single cell and the most complex creatures there are various levels of living beings and their organisation. In the creation of every level and every organisation there is perfection and harmony, and for each there are individual duties and collective purposes. The hand of power makes them carry out this work in an inspired manner, and this profound truth, namely the work of creation and proportioning, is a witness that is just (shahid 'adl) upon the whole universe.

The human heart can attain this truth provided it is ready to derive the indications of this universe and reflects upon the existents of the universe with an open heart. Whatever the level of a person's acquired knowledge, and whether he is a member of an advanced society or of a backward society, he can derive these inspired indications from the things of the universe, provided the windows of his heart and mind are also ready to receive these indications and are open, and provided some strings of reason and wisdom are fit to respond with melody to the plectrum of truth.

After this come the observation of the universe and various sciences, and the human being, in the study of nature, receives from the first glance an inspiration, and all observations confirm it. Some people, through observing the universe, have gathered such indications as lift the veil from the face of the collective truth hidden within this universe.

Mr. Chrissie Morrison, president of the Academy of Scientific Sciences of New York, records his observations in his book "Man Does Not Stand Alone" as follows:

"Birds have a faculty of returning home. A certain sparrow that builds its nest on doorways migrates south in the autumn season and returns to the same place in the spring of the following year. In the month of September most of the birds of America travel south, and flying over seas and deserts they cover thousands of miles, and never lose their way. And homing pigeons travel long distances in cages, and when they are released with a message they circle for a while in bewilderment, and after that they fly straight towards their homeland, and never stray from the path. If a honeybee goes somewhere and the traces of its path are erased by some storm, it still does not lose its way and comes straight back to the hive. However, in man this instinct is weak, and man makes up for this deficiency through his instruments and reason. Tiny insects also have extremely small and microscopic eyes, and these are most perfect eyes. The eyes of hawks and eagles and the like are like binoculars; the human eye cannot compete with them. This deficiency too has been made up by human reason and experience. Thus through these binoculars man sees the stars, and he has increased the sharpness of human vision a million-fold for seeing them. Moreover, man has invented such microscopes through which he sees bacteria and other creatures that are not visible to the eye."

"Now just let your old horse loose on the road. However dark it may be, it will not lose its way. It can see even in deep darkness, though perhaps not very clearly. It can see the temperature on the road and on both sides of it. Its eyes perceive this temperature through infrared rays. The owl can see a warm mouse moving beneath cold grass even when it is pitch dark, and humans have turned the dark night into day through the lights of electric bulbs."

"The world of honeybees is also wondrous. The worker bees construct different kinds of chambers in the hive. These are used for rearing. Small chambers are used for the workers and large chambers for the males, and special chambers are prepared for the queen. The queen, when she lays an unfertilised egg, places it in the chamber of the males, and when she lays a fertilised egg, she places it in the chamber in which the female worker bees are, who will in time become queen bees; and the worker bees, which are labourers, when they have performed the task of producing offspring for a long time, are replaced. These worker bees also perform the task of preparing food for the young. They chew honey and pollen and make them digestible, and when the sex of the young becomes manifest, they cease the process of preparing food in the above-mentioned manner. After this they are given honey and pollen-dust, and among the young those females who are trained in this manner later become worker bees."

As for the female bees that are in the cells of the queen bees, the feeding of them with honey and pollen-dust, made digestible in the initial stage, continues, and those female bees who are treated in this way later become queen bees. Only this queen lays eggs that are fertilised. In accordance with this technology, the young that are born require special kinds of cells, a special kind of egg, and a special kind of food. And the effect of the change in food is also wondrous. For this technology, the bees must have needed a long period of waiting, during which they distinguished these principles, applied them, and learned the effects of food, and applied collectively what was necessary for their existence. When the bees began their collective life, they must have then learned these principles, because for the existence of the bee and the preservation of its life these principles did not need to be discovered. Therefore it appears that the honeybee has researched the effects of food more than man has."

(The author, immersed in Western thought, is not prepared to accept that when Allah created the bee He taught it all this. Darwin's philosophy of evolution sits upon their minds, whereas the Qur'an clearly says: "And He taught Adam the names, all of them" — Allah taught Adam all the names; in the same way Allah gave the bee all its basic instruction. (Translator.))

"The dog has been given an additional nose through which it smells every animal that has passed along a path. Human olfactory power is weak in comparison with dogs, and to this day man has not invented any instrument that develops his sense of smell. Yet even this weak sense of smell of ours perceives such tiny particles as can be seen only through a microscope."

Most animals hear sounds that cannot cause vibration in the eardrums of our ears, because these are too subtle and fine for the limit of our hearing. Man has invented such instruments that he can hear even the sound of the wings of a fly flying miles away, as though it were sitting on the eardrum of his ear. By such instruments the sound of the speed of the sun's rays is also being recorded."

"There is a kind of water spider which builds a nest under water like a balloon. It is made of spider silk, and it is fastened to something beneath the water. Then this spider carries bubbles of water with the hairs of its body and takes them and attaches them to the nest, until a barrier of air bubbles forms around the nest. After that it lays its young inside the nest so that they remain safe from the storm of air. In the structure of this nest there is, on the one hand, the process of fine weaving, and after that, deep engineering and a profound understanding of aeronautics."

Salmon, which are small fish, spend several years roaming the sea, and then return to the river where they were born. What is the force that guides them back to their birthplace? If one, while heading toward its birthplace, enters a wrong river, it immediately knows that this river is not its birthplace. So it moves within the river and, swimming against the current, reaches its destination.

The case of sea serpents is very strange, and their story is the opposite of the salmon's. When the life of this creature of God is complete, it travels from various ponds and rivers toward the deep seas. If they are in Europe, they cover thousands of miles and head to the depths of South Bermuda. There they lay eggs and die. Their offspring, when born, know only that they are in very deep waters. Yet these young follow the same route to the shore that their mother took when she came from the shore to the water. From the shore they then go to some river, canal, pool or pond. Thus every kind of water is suitable for sea serpents, because they have seen and faced great waves, storms and ocean turbulence. They travel along the coasts, and when they are fully grown, some hidden law compels them to return and go back to the deep seas. The question is: where does this urge arise within them? It has never happened that a hunter or fisherman caught an American sea serpent in European seas, or that a European serpent came into the net of an American fisherman. Because the European sea serpent must travel a long distance to the deep seas, nature gave it a long life of one year, or even more, so that it could reach its destined goal before dying, since the European sea serpent must cover a greater distance than the American one. Just look: what atoms and what molecules are these? When sea serpents gather in the form of fish, how does such a power of will arise within them that makes them undertake such distant journeys?

When the female moth enters through a ventilator of your home, carried by the wind, she sends a signal to her male, however far he may be. Sometimes he is very far away. He receives that signal and responds to it. No matter how hard a human tries to mislead it, it is impossible for it to make a mistake. Is there a radio station with them, or does that male have a radio or machine that receives signals from her? Let alone an aerial, is there an ether through which she creates vibrations? Our telephones and radios are rapid communication devices, but they connect one place to another through wires. In this way, this moth is superior to us.

Plants, without knowledge or intention, make use of many things to maintain their existence. For example, insects carry pollen to them; the wind does the same work; wild animals and birds also do this work, scattering their pollen and seeds. In the end, these plants also ensnared humans in their net. Humans gave beauty to nature, and nature gave them their reward. But humans also do not stop at any limit. Humans believe in *hal min mazid* (is there more?). They plowed, sowed seed, harvested, filled storehouses, then developed the crops, pruned branches and arranged food supplies. If they gave up this work, they would die of hunger, civilization and culture would end, and humanity would return to the Stone Age.

In many water creatures, such as the prawn, if one of its arms is cut off, it knows that a part of its body has been lost. Its cells and genes begin to rebuild that organ, and when the organ is complete, the cells stop this work and know that their duty has ended.

Water worms that have many legs, when they are split into two pieces, complete themselves using one of the pieces. If you cut off the head of this worm, it creates a second head.

We can heal wounds, but our surgeons still do not know how to activate cells so that they can create a new arm, or produce flesh, nails and nerves, if that were possible.

And there is another marvel: if a cell divides into two complete parts in its early days, two complete animals are produced from it. We see that twins are alike in appearance. This can be explained by the fact that in the early stage of pregnancy the cell divided, and from this it is also understood that in the early stage the cell is a complete individual, and similarly an individual exists in every cell.

In another chapter, this same author writes:

"The brown seed of the oak tree falls to the ground. Its brown shell protects it, and it tumbles and gets lodged in a crack in the earth. In the spring season its inner germ awakens. It breaks open that shell and draws nourishment from the kernel that has been stored inside the shell, within which lie its hereditary genes. Its roots go into the earth. You see that this plant emerges, becomes a small tree, and then becomes a complete tree. It contains many millions of genes. Until it resembles, in its roots, shell, fruit, trunk and branches, the tree from which that seed came. Millions of years ago, the oak tree that came into being produced fruits that to this day maintain the arrangement of their particles in the same way as the first oak fruit did."

This same author, in a third chapter, writes: "Every cell that is produced in a living creature is obliged to adapt itself so that it becomes a part of flesh or a part of skin, and either perishes, or becomes the shine of a tooth, or becomes the liquid matter of the eye, or becomes the nose and ears. Every cell adapts itself into a form so that it fully performs its designated duty. It is extremely difficult for anyone to determine which cell belongs to the right hand or the left hand. But by nature it is determined that this cell belongs to the right ear and that cell to the left ear. In short, thousands of cells are driven so that they do the right work, at the right time and in the right place."

In a fourth chapter, this person says: "Among various kinds of creatures, some perform works that reflect the highest level of wisdom, whose explanation we cannot provide. For example, the wasp hunts the grasshopper. It digs a pit in the earth and buries it in a suitable place. While hunting, it stings the grasshopper at such a specific point that it becomes unconscious, yet its flesh remains intact and alive. Now the female wasp lays her eggs at a fixed place near it. Perhaps she does not even know that when her young are born they will eat the flesh of this grasshopper, but they will not kill it, because this flesh is their food, and if the flesh spoiled it would become poisonous. Surely the wasp must have begun this work from the beginning, and she must always repeat it, otherwise the existence of wasps would have ended from the world. Science has no explanation that could state the cause of this continuous action of the wasps, and it is also not possible that the wasps do this work merely by chance, because the female wasp fills the pit she has dug in the earth and goes away and dies. Neither did her ancestors know why she does this, nor does she know or observe what her young will face afterward. Rather, the wasp does not even know that there is anything coming after her that she would call her child. It does not even know that she does this work for the protection of the species."

Among ants, some have the duty of gathering creatures to supply food to their colony during the winter season. Then they establish a store where this food is ground and kept. Then some ants are such that nature has given them grinding jaws. Their work is only to grind the food. When winter comes and all the grain has been ground, its supply is arranged so that the greatest possible number of ants benefit, so that the supply can continue. Now, since more grinding ants will be born in the next generation, the army of ants attacks those grinding ants and kills them. Perhaps their conscience is satisfied that they have eaten their share of food during the grinding, since they must have benefited from that opportunity.

Some ants are such that their instinct or their intelligence moves them to create gardens of food. These ants capture small insects and insects found on the shells of plants. These insects serve them like cows and goats. From these insects the ants take a liquid like honey, which serves as food for the ants.

Ants also enslave some other ants. When they build their nests, they cut leaves to a suitable size. When worker ants hold these leaves from one side and place them in position, they also make use of the young ants that are still in their developmental stage, using their silky material to join the leaves. Thus that young ant is deprived of building a nest for itself, yet it has already performed a useful task for its kind. The question is: how does the ability to do this work arise in the particles from which an ant is made? There is no doubt that there is a Creator who guided them to act in this way."

(Quotations end.)

There is no doubt that there is a Creator who gave guidance to all His creatures, whether they are large or small, and this is the same Creator who is ﴿the Most High…﴾ and guided (87:1–3): ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and proportioned, who determined and then guided.﴾

What we have quoted above are observations on only a small part of the reality, which humans have recorded regarding plants, insects, birds and other animals. But beyond this there are more worlds of knowledge and observation, and what is known to us is only a very small portion of the meaning and significance of this statement of God.

﴿Who created and proportioned, who determined and then guided﴾ (87:2–3). This observable universe, of which we know only a small part, has beyond it hidden worlds of the unseen. We have been given only a little knowledge according to our human capacities. These are a few indications that God has provided for our limited power of perception.

After presenting a broad page of this great universe and creating within its valleys the echo of God's glorification and praise, in order to complete this great tasbih of God, here a reference is made to the world of plants, and within this reference there is a world of meanings.

﴿And who brought forth the pasture, then made it dark stubble﴾ (87:4–5). *Al-mar'a* is applied to everything that grows from the earth, because every growing thing is food for some creature. Therefore, the meaning of *mar'a* here is far broader than saying that something is *mar'a* only if it is grazed by our livestock. God created the earth and, for every creature that moves upon this earth, provided its food within it, whether that creature moves on the earth, hides within it, or flies in its skies.

Plants are first green, then they wither and become dark. Sometimes they are fit for food while still green, and sometimes they ripen and become dark, and then they serve as food. Even in the intermediate state they serve as some kind of food. In any case, every state of plants becomes food for some creature, according to God's creation and proportioning.

By presenting the scene of plant life, a sign is given here that just as every plant ends up as rubbish, so every living creature also reaches its end in this world. This is also a sign pointing to this worldly life and the life of the Hereafter: that worldly life, like plants, is destined to end, while the life of the Hereafter remains and is everlasting. This comes later:

﴿But you prefer the worldly life, while the Hereafter is better and more lasting﴾ (87:16–17). Worldly life is like a field that ends and becomes rubbish, while the Hereafter is enduring and everlasting.

Through this closing passage, the pages of this great universe are spread out far and wide, and the matters mentioned are appropriate to the realities that come in this surah. This universe harmonizes with them, and these realities are woven into the universe. It is a very broad and expansive framework. If one studies deeply, the themes of this section of the Qur'an are presented within a vast cosmic scope. This cosmic scope harmonizes with the atmosphere of this portion and with its indications and themes.

Now comes the glad tidings that is for you, and after you, for your Ummah.

﴿Sanuqri'uka fa-la tansa﴾ ... ﴿illa ma sha'a Allah﴾ ... ﴿al-dhikra﴾

This great glad tiding begins with the removal of the burden of memorizing and preserving the Qur'an from the shoulders of the Prophet ﷺ.

﴿Sanuqri'uka fa-la tansa﴾ (87:6) "We shall make you recite, so you will not forget." Therefore, take this speech from your Lord and be content. Making you remember it is Allah's task. This was indeed a great glad tiding for the Prophet ﷺ. He was anxious about memorizing the Qur'an. Now he was reassured about its preservation by Allah, because the Qur'an is an extremely great speech and you held it very dear. You were devoted to the Qur'an with heart and soul, took great care of its preservation, were eager for it, and regarded it as your great and heavy responsibility. You used to repeat every verse. When Jibril (peace be upon him) brought it, you would repeat it along with listening, and occupied your tongue with repeating it, until this good news came and you were reassured.

Then, after you, it is also a glad tiding for your Ummah. The Ummah too is reassured that the true source of this belief is the Divine Being, and that the guardian and responsible one for its preservation is also Allah: responsible for implanting it in the heart of the Prophet and responsible for its preservation in the later times. This is a great mercy of Allah, and a proof of the greatness of this religion and of its importance in the sight of Allah.

On this occasion, and on all such occasions, one firm matter certainly comes forward. This is a firm and perpetual law: that Allah's will is unrestricted, and there is no constraint upon Allah's will. You will not forget, except what Allah wishes to make you forget. This restriction, even though it comes from Allah Himself, means that Allah's will is unbounded and no legal bond binds it, and no promise binds it. The Qur'an preserves this principle fully, as we have already explained in Zilal al-Qur'an earlier. Here too this principle has been maintained.

﴿Illa ma sha'a Allah﴾ (87:7) "Except what Allah wills." Although the promise is true that the Messenger will not forget, Allah's will is also unrestricted; if Allah wills, it may happen, so that all matters remain within the scope of Allah's will, and people keep their gaze fixed on Allah's will alone, even where a true promise has been made in a matter. The human heart and mind must remain attached to Allah's will alone.

﴿Innahu ya'lamu al-jahra wa ma yakhfa﴾ (87:7) "He knows what is apparent and what is hidden." This is the indication that Allah will teach, will cause memorization, and there will be no forgetting, except what He wishes otherwise, because all these matters are based on Allah's hidden wisdom, who knows the apparent and the secret, and knows matters from all their aspects; therefore He makes decisions in all matters that contain wisdom, and this wisdom is based on Allah's complete knowledge. Allah's knowledge is perfect knowledge.

Now the second glad tiding: ﴿Wa nuyassiruka li-l-yusra﴾ (87:8) "And We will ease you toward the easy way." This glad tiding is also for the sacred person of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and after you, it is also for your Ummah. From it we also learn the nature of this religion, the reality of the Islamic call, what role it plays in human life, and what position the Islamic system of life holds in this universe. Apparently these are only two words.

﴿Wa nuyassiruka li-l-yusra﴾ (87:8) But the reality stated within them is a great reality of the Islamic worldview, the Islamic system, and the Shari'ah; and moreover it is the summary and spirit of this entire universe. This reality joins the temperament of the Messenger of Allah with the temperament of this universe and the temperament of this religion. This whole universe has been made very easily by the hand of power. This universe is running with great ease; on whatever course it has been set, it moves along that course and direction with great comfort, tranquility and facility. In short, it has come forth from light, and points toward realities that lie beyond limits and bounds.

The one whom Allah makes easy in things walks easily on the paths of his life. He walks with this universe, whose existence and whose arrangement are proportionate to each other, whose movement is balanced and whose direction is one: toward Allah. Such a person clashes only with those forces which deviate from the lines of this great universe. If the weight of such people is compared with this entire universe, they have no weight left. When such a person moves, his movement is easy, subtle and gentle, in harmony with the universe, in harmony with the events of the world, in harmony with the things and persons of the world. There is ease in his hands, ease in his tongue, his initiatives are easy, his action is ease. His thoughts are easy, his thinking is easy; he takes matters easily, takes matters with great ease, is easy for himself and easy for others.

This was the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: ease upon ease in all his affairs. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had to choose between two matters, he would take the easier. This is the narration of Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her). (Bukhari and Muslim)

And from her also is narrated: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was alone in his house, he was gentle-natured with all people, smiling and laughing." And a narration in Sahih Bukhari: "A maidservant would take hold of the hand of the Messenger of Allah and lead him wherever she wished."

If one reflects on his conduct regarding clothing, food, bedding and so on, it becomes clear that he preferred simplicity, ease and lack of formality. Abu Abdullah Shams al-Din Muhammad ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyyah, in his book Zad al-Ma'ad, writes regarding the Prophet's conduct in clothing that he had a turban called "al-Sahab," which he gave to Ali (may Allah be pleased with him). He would tie a turban and wear a cap beneath it; sometimes he wore a cap without a turban, and sometimes he tied a turban without a cap. When he tied his turban he would let its end hang between the two shoulders, as in the narration of Sahih Muslim. Umar ibn Huraith narrates that he saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on the pulpit wearing a black turban, with one end hanging between his two shoulders. And in Muslim, from Jabir, there is also: "like a lock of hair."

From this it is known that he did not always let the end hang between the shoulders. It is said that when he entered Makkah, he wore battle attire and had a helmet on his head. Thus he wore clothing suited to each occasion.

In another section he states: the best way is the way of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, which he established, commanded, encouraged, and maintained. In clothing, his practice was to wear whatever clothing was available: sometimes woolen, sometimes cotton, sometimes linen. He wore a Yemeni cloak, a green cloak, and also wore a hullah, qaba and qamis. He wore trousers, izar and a sheet. Leather socks and shoes. He used all these things, and sometimes he let the end of the turban hang behind and sometimes he did not.

And regarding food, his practice was that he would not reject any food present, nor would he stand on ceremony regarding absent food; of pure things, whatever was presented to him he would eat. Unless his disposition did not desire some thing, in which case he left it without declaring it unlawful. He never found fault with any food. If he desired it he ate, otherwise he left it, as he did not eat the lizard, because he was not accustomed to eating it; yet he did not declare it unlawful for the Ummah, and it was eaten at his table in his presence. He ate halwa and honey, which he liked very much. He ate fresh and dried dates. He drank pure milk and mixed milk. He took honey and sawiq with water. He drank clear date-water. He used harira, which is a kind of pudding made from milk and flour. He ate cucumber with fresh dates, ate cheese, ate bread with dates, ate bread with vinegar. He ate cooked pumpkin and liked it very much. He ate boiled pumpkin, ate thareed with ghee, ate cheese. He ate bread with oil, ate melons with fresh dates and dates with butter, and this was very dear to him. He would not reject any pure thing, nor would he desire something with formality; rather his way was to eat whatever was available, and if nothing was available he would be patient."

Regarding sleeping and waking, his Sunnah was this: sometimes he slept on his bed, sometimes on a hide, sometimes on a mat, sometimes on the ground, sometimes on a couch, sometimes on a black blanket.

From his sayings it is known that gentleness should be practiced in all matters, among which come the Islamic worldview and its requirements. Regarding this, his instructions are very many; it is difficult to bring them all here, a few are presented: "This religion is easy, and whoever wrestles with this religion will be defeated." (Bukhari). "Do not be harsh upon yourselves, lest you be dealt with harshly; a people made themselves harsh and so they were dealt with harshly." (Abu Dawud). "Whoever is harsh with his mount, neither can he complete the journey nor does his mount remain alive." (Bukhari). "Make things easy, do not make them difficult." (Bukhari and Muslim).

And his instructions regarding dealings are these: "May Allah have mercy on the one who sells with gentleness and generosity, buys with gentleness and generosity, and demands with gentleness and generosity." (Bukhari). "The believer is easy and gentle." (Bayhaqi). "The believer is sociable and people feel at ease with him." (Daraqutni). "The most hated person before Allah is the one who is quarrelsome and contentious." (Bukhari and Muslim).

In his biography there are clear examples that he did not like harshness and difficulty, even in names and in features of the face. This whole universe has been made very easily by the hand of power. In short, it has come forth from light, and points toward realities that lie beyond limits and bounds.

﴿The nature of Allah upon which He created mankind; there is no change in the creation of Allah﴾ (30:30).

When a person wishes to live his life with this belief, he finds it very easy. He sees that human strength has been taken into consideration in it, that the various circumstances of a person have been observed in it, and that the conditions a person encounters in different kinds of societies have also been kept in mind. The Islamic belief itself is extremely simple and comprehensible: there is the belief in one God, and there is nothing like Him. All creatures have been created by that same God, and that same God has also told them the purpose of their creation. Then He sent Messengers, and these Messengers informed people of their purpose of existence. The Messengers returned people to their innate nature (khalq). Countless examples of this exist in his biography. This is precisely the matter that is stated to him in this verse as glad tidings, and in his whole life, in his call and in his affairs, he was granted the ability to do it.

﴿Wa nuyassiruka li-l-yusra﴾ (87:8) "And We will make it easy for you to follow the easy religion."

The personality of the Messenger ﷺ, who was beloved by creation and endowed with noble character, and who had been guided to an easy religion with ease, so he treated people in just this manner. And in this same way he invited humanity. His temperament became exactly this way, and his very nature was transformed into the easy religion, and he became capable of bearing this great trust (al-amanah al-kubra). This trust was indeed very great and heavy, but Allah granted him the ability to shoulder this responsibility, and he became capable of carrying this heavy burden. He acted in a commendable manner and labored in a good way, and he worked with joy and expansiveness of heart.

Many verses of the Qur'an have also been revealed in praise of the Messenger ﷺ and in explanation of the nature of his work.

﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ (al-Anbiya 21:107). ﴿Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered prophet, whom they find written in what they have of the Torah and the Gospel, who enjoins upon them what is right and forbids them what is wrong, makes lawful for them the good things and prohibits for them the evil things, and relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them﴾ (al-A'raf 7:157). Therefore the mission of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was a mercy for all of humanity. He came and removed the burdens from the shoulders of people and the shackles from their necks which they had placed upon themselves, and this was because they had been severe in religion, so Allah was severe upon them in return. The Qur'an also says about the religion and the call that he brought:

﴿And We have indeed made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there anyone who will remember?﴾ (al-Qamar 54:22). And elsewhere: ﴿And He has not placed upon you any hardship in religion﴾ (al-Hajj 22:78). And in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ (2:286). And in al-Ma'idah: ﴿Allah does not intend to put upon you any difficulty, but He intends to purify you﴾ (5:6).

In short, this final message is easy and within the bounds of human capacity. Allah has not subjected people to hardship, nor is it Allah's intention to put people into hardship; rather, ease is present in the spirit of Islam and ease has been kept in view in the rulings of Islam. In short, this is a natural religion. In Surat al-Rum:

﴿The nature of Allah upon which He created mankind; there is no change in the creation of Allah﴾ (30:30).

When a person wishes to live his life with this belief, he finds it very easy. He sees that human strength has been taken into consideration in it, that the various circumstances of a person have been observed in it, and that the conditions a person encounters in different kinds of societies have also been kept in mind. The Islamic belief itself is extremely simple and comprehensible: there is the belief in one God, and there is nothing like Him. All creatures have been created by that same God, and that same God has also told them the purpose of their creation. Then He sent Messengers, and these Messengers informed people of their purpose of existence. The Messengers returned people to their innate nature (khalq). After that, whatever obligations were imposed upon them arise from this same view, in a most straightforward and simple manner, in which there is no crookedness. And people were commanded that they should act upon those commands which they are able to act upon, without harshness and hardship. The Prophet ﷺ said: "When I command you with something, carry it out as much as you are able, and whatever I forbid you, abstain from it." (Bukhari and Muslim). And from among the things that have been prohibited, the state of necessity (idtirar) is excepted:

﴿Except what you are compelled to, while it is [still] lawful﴾ (al-An'am 6:119).

Thus the nature of the Messenger of the Last Age ﷺ became intermingled with his messengership and his call, and the reality of the call and the caller became one, especially in this fundamental quality and this distinctive hue. In the same way, this ummah too was called the middle and easy ummah, the ummah to which the Messenger of Allah brought this message. It was an ummah upon which mercy descended, and it rose carrying the message of mercy and love to show people the most easy and straight path. In such a way that the temperament of this ummah became a universal and cosmic temperament, and a deep harmony came about between its temperament and the temperament of this vast universe.

Now reflect upon this universe: how smooth and flowing is the movement of its motion, and there is no collision or conflict in it. Billions and trillions of celestial bodies float in this cosmic space, flowing in their respective orbits with perfect harmony, with perfect proportion and a pleasing attraction, within which there is no turbulence. Not one of them deviates from its orbit. Billions and trillions of living creatures live their lives on this earth and fulfill their immediate purposes, and this life passes with great firmness and tremendous organization. Everything fulfills its purpose of creation with great ease and proceeds on its appointed path towards its destination. In this universe, billions and trillions of movements, events and conditions are taking place, gathered and scattered, and all of them are moving along one path, just as a group of musicians produces entirely different sounds from their respective instruments, and all these different sounds form one melody and create a long symphony. The truth is that there is a tremendous harmony between the existence of this universe, the Islamic system of life, the biography of the Messenger ﷺ, and the temperament of the Muslim ummah, because this is the workmanship of Allah, the nature described by Allah, and the melody of Allah, and He is the most Wise Craftsman.

﴿So remind, if the reminder benefits﴾ (al-A'la 87:9). Allah taught the Prophet ﷺ and guaranteed that he would not forget, except what Allah wills. Then Allah facilitated for the Prophet ﷺ an easy path so that he could bear the weight of this great trust with ease and remind people. For this reason he was prepared and given glad tidings, and it was said that whenever an opportunity arises, he should remind, whenever he finds a way to place the matter into hearts, and whenever the means of conveying are available. Here it is said:

﴿If the reminder benefits﴾ (al-A'la 87:9): whenever you remind, there should continuously be benefit. It never happens that a reminder benefits no one, whether little or much; no generation has ever been empty of those who benefit. Even if corruption becomes widespread in the age, hearts become rusted, and veils fall over them, nevertheless reminder does benefit.

When we reflect on the sequence of these verses, we learn the greatness of prophethood and realize how great and important this trust is. For the fulfillment of this duty, Allah guided to an easy method and provided facilities: first He made him remember, then He took on the responsibility of protecting this message so that the Messenger of Allah could carry out the duty of reminding with tranquility, and then He commanded that he remind if it is beneficial. All these facilities were given and then he was set to work, and this was in fact a great provision for the journey.

When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ completed his duty, his task was finished. Then people are free and their affairs are their own. After conveying and reminding, people's paths, their goals and their outcomes become different. It is Allah who brings some to one end and others to another, according to the attitude they adopted in accepting or rejecting.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 87, verse 10:

"So remind, [O Prophet], if the reminder benefits."

Your reminder will be benefited from only by the one who fears [Allah].

Man yakhshā (87:10): the one in whose heart there is the fear of Allah, who fears the displeasure of Allah and the punishment of Allah. Only the person who is alive, and who knows that there is a Creator of this universe, who created this world and made it perfectly balanced, determined its destiny and guided people to the right path, fears and remains cautious. He has not left people as unrestrained beasts, nor created them without purpose. Therefore, concerning good and evil, Allah is the Reckoner, and He judges with justice and fairness. Such a person fears Allah, and when he is given advice, he takes heed; when insight is given to him, he accepts it, and when he is admonished, he takes a lesson from it.

And he will avoid it, the most wretched one (87:11). Whoever is wretched will turn away from admonition. Such a person will neither listen to a word of advice nor benefit from it; he is wretched, wretched absolutely, one in whom wretchedness has reached its highest degree, that is, the most wretched. He is wretched because of his debased soul, wretched because he does not perceive the realities of this universe, wretched because he does not comprehend the signs present within this universe, wretched because he fails to grasp the indications of the cosmos. He is also wretched in that he pursues with great greed the trivial interests of this world, exhausting himself for them, and wretched in the Hereafter, where his lot will be the everlasting Hellfire, whose ages will have no end.

The Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 87, verses 12–13:

الذی .................... ولا یحی (13:87) "Who will enter the greatest Fire, and then he will neither die therein nor live."

What is this greatest Fire? It is the Fire of Hell. Its intensity will be great, its periods (of punishment) will be long, its extent will be vast, and the stay in it will be prolonged. In it one will neither die and so be free from the feeling of torment, nor live in a way that brings comfort. Rather, it will be an everlasting punishment, and there the people will long for death in the same way that here people die pursuing great desires. In contrast to this, there is deliverance, success, purity, and admonition.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 87, verses 14–15:

"He indeed succeeds who purifies himself, and remembers the name of his Lord, and prays." (87:14–15)

Tazkiyah (purification) means to purify oneself from every filth and every sin. In this verse, Allah decides that whoever purifies himself, causes the majesty of his Lord to settle in his heart, and then prays, or fears Allah and obeys, has succeeded. Both meanings renew the remembrance of Allah, the majesty settles in the heart, and awe of Allah is born in the conscience. So the decision is that such a person will attain success. In this world too he will attain success: his heart will be attached to Allah and alive, he will feel sweetness in the remembrance of Allah, and he will have intimacy with the Creator. And in the Hereafter too he will attain success: he will be saved from the great Fire, and he will be in the everlasting bliss of the Gardens. The end of both has been stated, and between the ends of the two there is "the distance between the two easts" (bu'd al-mashriqayn).

In this frightening scene, in which the Great Fire (al-nar al-kubra) is shown, and in contrast to it, the scene of salvation is shown for those who adopt purification. After these scenes, it is explained why people become entangled in the grip of misfortune, what the real cause of their heedlessness is, and what prevents them from admonition, purification, and success and salvation. And what is the thing that casts them into Hell and makes them wretched.

Truly, you prefer the worldly life, (87:16)

Indeed, the root of every calamity is love of the world. For this reason a person turns away from admonition, because the demand of the Hereafter is this: be mindful of it and give precedence to the Hereafter. And there are people who seek the world and give it priority.

This world is not called "dunya" merely as a name; rather, it is "dunya dani" (the lowly world): near, and quickly passing away. In comparison, the Hereafter is good, better, and enduring.

﴿And the Hereafter is better and more enduring﴾ (87:17). By its very nature it is enduring, good, and continuing forever and ever. Therefore those who prefer the world over the Hereafter are committing great folly, and their approach is wrong. It is not the work of an intelligent and perceptive person.

At the end, it is explained that the Islamic call is not a new call; it has a long history. From the beginning of creation and from the existence of humanity, this call has been ongoing, and its principles transcend the bounds of time and place.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 87, verses 18–19:

ان ھذا ............................ موسیٰ

The themes that have come in this surah are the fundamental principles of this great creed, and these are the same fundamental principles of da'wah (the call to faith) and the principles of religion that were mentioned in the books and scriptures of Prophet Musa (peace be upon him) and Prophet Ibrahim (peace be upon him).

That truth is one, the creed is one, and the principles of religion are one: this is the testimony that all these religions are from one God. It is one and the same will and purpose (mashiyyah) that willed Ibrahim and Musa (peace be upon them both), and then willed the mission of Hadrat Muhammad (ﷺ). Truth is one, so its source is also one. Yes, there are differences in the secondary matters (furu') of the religions, but these exist because God, in the laws and legislation (shari'ah), made changes in accordance with the circumstances and requirements of the time. However, the origin of all the shara'i' (divine laws) is one, and all the shari'ahs emerged from one source, namely they came from that same Most High Lord who created man and made him proportionate, who ordained everything and determined its destiny (taqdir), and who guided everything.
